title: 3-Read Friday #23: Lesson Pace, Productive Struggle, and Mathematical Miscellany
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 23 opens with an unusually candid admission from Barton: he's given the same vague improve-your-pace lesson-observation feedback that Adam Robbins's post dismantles, and he credits Robbins with identifying the two underlying problems that make pace an unhelpful piece of feedback. His second pick, Greg Ashman's "Is productive struggle ethical?", is framed against Barton's own earlier enthusiasm for productive struggle in his book How I Wish I'd Taught Maths, with Barton noting his own experience that struggle sometimes backfires and turns students off before they've engaged with an idea, and crediting Ashman's PhD research for tackling the question head-on. He closes with a lighter selection, Colleen Young's "Mathematical Miscellany #91," a curated roundup of maths teaching resources that Barton flags explicitly as a treat for the maths geeks rather than an argument-driven piece. Across the issue, Barton's own editorial voice is more exposed than usual, twice positioning the picks as correctives to positions he has personally held.
points: Barton opens with a personal confession about having given the exact vague improve-your-pace feedback that Adam Robbins's post critiques, giving the pick unusual editorial vulnerability.

His framing of Greg Ashman's productive-struggle piece links back to his own book How I Wish I'd Taught Maths, positioning Ashman's PhD-informed skepticism as a challenge to an idea Barton himself once found appealing.

He closes the issue with Colleen Young's resource-roundup post, explicitly bucketing it as a treat for the maths geeks rather than a substantive argument piece, signalling a lighter register for the third slot.
The issue's throughline is professional self-correction: two of three picks directly revisit ideas Barton or the wider profession once endorsed and are now reconsidering.
quotes: Confession time: in my early years of giving feedback following lesson observations, I have definitely uttered the phrase “You need to improve the pace of the lesson” several times.

Only now do I realise just how utterly meaningless and unactionable such feedback is. Adam hits the nail on the head in this post, identifying two fundamental problems that occur when discussing the pace of a lesson.

The idea sounds great - give students a problem to wrestle with to motivate them to want to learn how to solve it. But my experience has been that for some students such struggle has the exact opposite effect, and turns them off the new idea
Greg has tackled this issue for his PhD, and reflects on his key findings in this post.
Colleen does a fantastic series of posts where she picks out her favourite resources and ideas she has recently seen.
This latest collection is a cracker, with worked example animations, Venn diagrams, curriculum resources, and a set of free classroom activities from Eedi.
